St. Ignatius Brianchaninov

St. Ignatius Brianchaninov

Period

Region

Titles / vocation
Hierarch · Monastic
Commemoration

Introduction

St. Ignatius Brianchaninov is the Russian bishop and ascetical author whose life passes from military education into monastic leadership.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Peaceful repose in his cell, April 30, 1867.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The OCA describes noble family origins, studies in Saint Petersburg, and a struggle to obtain release from the expected military career.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 1; Published biographical account,paragraph 2; Published biographical account,paragraph 3

Life and notable events

After formation under elders, he serves at Saint Sergius Hermitage and later as bishop of the Caucasus and Stavropol, then retires to Babaev Monastery.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 24; Published biographical account,paragraph 30; Published biographical account,paragraph 31; Published biographical account,paragraph 35

Deputatov’s account follows Ignatius from military engineering through illness and discharge to four years as a novice. It singles out his bond with Leonid of Optina. It then relates the emperor’s intervention in his appointment to Saint Sergius Hermitage, and describes the twenty-four years spent rebuilding the community before episcopal consecration in 1857.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 4; Published biographical account,paragraph 7

Retirement did not end the practical work described by the OCA. At Babaev he improved buildings, finances, the use of land, and the monastery’s internal order. The account also records visits from close associates and imperial visitors, including AlexanderII in 1866. It shows his final years combining revision of manuscripts, correspondence, and continuing responsibility for a community.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 34; Published biographical account,paragraph 35; Published biographical account,paragraph 36; Published biographical account,paragraph 37

Death and martyrdom

The life describes peaceful repose in his cell on April 30, 1867; it does not claim that witnesses observed the moment of death.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 41

Writings and legacy

It records glorification in 1988 and his relics at Tolga. Deputatov’s separately published account below describes the writings and the return to literary work in retirement.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 30; Published biographical account,paragraph 42 · [2] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 3; Published biographical account,paragraph 27

The same publication describes retirement after four years as bishop, the editing of earlier articles, and extensive correspondence with spiritual children. It identifies The Arena, the ascetical collections, the Patericon, and writing on death among the literary legacy. Its opening credits the translated selection to Deputatov’s The Awareness of God. The translated spiritual sayings that follow are not reproduced as if their English wording were public domain.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 3; Published biographical account,paragraph 7; Published biographical account,paragraph 8; Published biographical account,paragraph 13

Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.

Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.

Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.

Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all.

Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.

Related Scripture; not a claim that this passage narrates the saint’s life or is a prescribed feast-day reading.

[3] Public-domain Bible translation · 1Tim 4: 12–16

Deputatov introduces the collected writings as material grounded in the Fathers. His account gives the English reader a bibliographic starting point while retaining the difference between an author’s life and a personalized ascetic program.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 3
